title: Arrays and Tuples
summary: TypeScript can describe the values in a list. A tuple also describes what kind of value belongs in each position.
introduction: TypeScript can describe the values in a list. A tuple also describes what kind of value belongs in each position. Use a number list for scores. Then try a pair that holds a name and a score, where each position has its own job.
learningObjectives: Declare typed and readonly arrays and read the errors for wrong element types
Use tuple types with labelled positions for fixed-length results
Explain what noUncheckedIndexedAccess changes and when to use as const

blocks.text: `number[]` and `Array<number>` mean the same thing; the first is shorter and more common, the second shows that arrays are generic (the [generics lesson](/tutorials/typescript/generics) explains the angle brackets). The element type is enforced on every write: `push`, index assignment, `unshift` and `splice` all check their arguments.

blocks.title: arrays.ts
npx tsc arrays.ts
blocks.content:
arrays.ts:10:13 - error TS2345: Argument of type 'string' is not assignable to parameter of type 'number'.

10 scores.push("95");
               ~~~~


Found 1 error in arrays.ts:10

blocks.text: Without the last line the file prints `Ada, Grace, Linus 91.7`. The `reduce` callback needs no annotations: `sum` and `s` are inferred from the array's element type and the initial value `0`. Note that `const` protects the *binding*, not the contents; `scores.push(100)` is allowed on a `const` array.

`readonly number[]` removes every mutating method from the type. Accepting readonly arrays in function parameters is a strong signal to callers that their data will not be changed. Non-mutating methods such as `map`, `filter` and `slice` still work and return ordinary, mutable arrays whose element type is inferred from the callback.

blocks.title: readonly.ts
npx tsc readonly.ts
blocks.content:
readonly.ts:8:8 - error TS2339: Property 'push' does not exist on type 'readonly number[]'.

8 primes.push(7);
         ~~~~


Found 1 error in readonly.ts:8

blocks.text: Hover over `doubled` and `labels`: they are `number[]` and `string[]` respectively, derived from what each callback returns. Running the file without the last line prints `[ 4, 6, 10 ] [ '#2', '#3', '#5' ]`.

A tuple is an array with a fixed length and a known type for each position, written as a list in square brackets. Since TypeScript 4.0 you can label the positions (`[x: number, y: number]`); labels document the meaning and appear in hover text but do not change the runtime array. Tuples are ideal for returning two values from a function and destructuring them.

blocks.title: tuples.ts
npx tsc tuples.ts
blocks.content:
tuples.ts:12:7 - error TS2322: Type '[number, number, number]' is not assignable to type 'Point'.
  Source has 3 element(s) but target allows only 2.

12 const bad: Point = [1, 2, 3];
         ~~~


Found 1 error in tuples.ts:12

blocks.text: The working part prints `[ 0, 0 ] 1 9`. Destructuring `const [low, high] = minMax(...)` gives `low` and `high` the type `number` straight from the tuple positions. Tuples may also have optional positions (`[string, number?]`) and a rest element (`[string, ...number[]]`) for lists with a fixed head and a variable tail.

Reading `colors[2]` from an array of two strings returns `undefined` at runtime, yet the type of the expression is `string`. By default TypeScript assumes every index is in range, because checking for `undefined` after every array access would make simple loops noisy.

blocks.title: index.ts
npx tsx index.ts (no compiler error with the default settings)
blocks.content: TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'toUpperCase')

blocks.title: Common mistake: trusting an index
blocks.text: Add `"noUncheckedIndexedAccess": true` to `compilerOptions` and the same file fails to compile with `index.ts:4:13 - error TS18048: 'third' is possibly 'undefined'.` The option makes every element read from an array or index signature `T | undefined`, which forces a check such as `third?.toUpperCase()` or an early return. It is one of the two extra checks that `tsc --init` enables in TypeScript 5.9. Turn it on for new projects; for lists you iterate with `for...of`, `map` or `filter` nothing changes, because those never produce an out-of-range element.

`["S", "M", "L"]` is inferred as `string[]`: the literal values are widened and the array stays mutable. Adding `as const` turns it into the readonly tuple `readonly ["S", "M", "L"]`, and the indexed access type `(typeof sizes)[number]` extracts the union of its elements. The array now serves two purposes: a runtime list to loop over and a compile-time type that stays in sync with it.

blocks.title: asconst.ts
npx tsc asconst.ts
blocks.content:
asconst.ts:10:7 - error TS2345: Argument of type '"XL"' is not assignable to parameter of type '"S" | "M" | "L"'.

10 order("XL");
         ~~~~


Found 1 error in asconst.ts:10

blocks.title: Which one to reach for
blocks.text: A list of things of the same kind: `T[]`. A fixed-shape result with different meanings per position: a labelled tuple. A fixed set of allowed values that you also need at runtime: `as const` plus `(typeof list)[number]`. A parameter you promise not to modify: `readonly T[]`.

questions.question: What is the inferred type of `const ids = [1, 2, 3].map((n) => String(n));`?
questions.explanation: map returns a new array whose element type is whatever the callback returns. String(n) returns a string, so the result is string[].

questions.question: With the default compiler settings, `const x = [10, 20][5];` gives `x` the type `number | undefined`.
questions.explanation: By default indexed access is assumed to be in range, so x is typed number even though it is undefined at runtime. Only noUncheckedIndexedAccess adds the undefined.
